name: Aisha Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Aisha. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Pinwheel Studio, a five-person agency in a converted shop on Harbour Road, and almost all our clients are cafés, restaurants and bars. So my week is menus, shopfront signs, logos, the odd delivery-app banner, and a lot of standing in kitchens measuring wall space. I like seeing a menu I laid out sitting on a real table with coffee rings on it. What wears me out is the last-minute price changes, because a chef will change one dish at 6pm and the whole menu has to go back to the printer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI tools in that work at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then, yes. I'll use an AI image tool to mock up a menu photo before we pay for a real shoot, or to clear the background off a product shot. I picked it up after Lewis, our junior, kept doing it faster than me. Farah, who owns the agency, is careful with it because restaurant owners want to feel they've paid for a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I say now, that it's a handy shortcut for the boring bits and nothing more. At work I'd probably joke that the robots still can't tell a chef his font is unreadable. Online I'd keep quiet, because designers arguing about AI is exhausting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, AI isn't my worry in this one, restaurants are. Two of our clients closed this year, the noodle bar and the bakery on Quay Street, When a café shuts, the menu work goes with it. My job is fine as long as Pinwheel's restaurant clients keep their doors open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the work and keep using the image tools for mockups, the way I do now. I'd also push Farah to take on a couple of non-food clients, like the dentist who asked about signage, so we're not all eggs in one basket. And I'd keep putting a bit into savings each month, because four months' rent isn't much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly normal, with a small knot about the restaurant side. It's the same worry I had last winter. Nothing about AI changes it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you nervous in that world, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether Pinwheel has a quiet spell, because if bills come first, my small cushion goes fast. Tom, my partner, earns steady money as a physio, so we wouldn't sink, but I'd hate leaning on him for my half of the rent. That's my line in the sand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If money did get tight, what goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the eating out, which is a bit funny given what I do. We go to client restaurants a lot, partly to check how my menus are holding up. I'd cut that down first and keep the savings going.

say: AI is a **handy shortcut** for mockups and background clean-up, nothing more.
Designers arguing online about AI is **exhausting**, so I'd mostly keep quiet about it.
think: My real risk is **restaurants closing**, not AI taking my work.
Two clients, the **noodle bar** and a bakery, already shut this year.
do: Keep using **image tools** for menu mockups as I do now.
Push Farah to take **non-food clients** like the dentist asking about signage.
Keep adding to **savings** every month beyond the current four months.
feel: Mostly normal, with a **small knot** about the restaurant trade.
S0.quote: When a café shuts, the menu work goes with it. My job is fine as long as Pinwheel's restaurant clients keep their doors open.
fieldNote: Her worry comes from the **client base**, not from technology, and she named the closed shops without prompting.
She'd rather cut **eating out** than ask her partner to cover her rent.
A steady, practical voice; she sees the agency's **concentration risk** more clearly than the tools.

steps.text: Keep making menu mockups with the AI image tool
Put a fixed amount into savings each payday
Cut client-restaurant dinners down to once a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need to get good at the tools before our clients do. With friends I'd probably say it's like when everyone got phones with good cameras: the jobs didn't vanish, they changed. I wouldn't post about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me more than I'd say. Half of what I do is the thinking side, writing menu descriptions, laying out price changes, sorting the print order, and that's exactly the list on your card. If a café owner can type their dishes into an app and get a decent menu, my boss Farah won't need three designers, and I'm the middle one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the paid course Farah keeps mentioning on the newer design tools, the one that's two evenings a week, and I'd use AI for the menu updates so I'm faster than an app. I'd also start learning sign installation and vinyl work from Marco, our printer, because someone still has to climb the ladder and fit it. And I'd not book the summer trip Tom and I were planning, and save that money instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy turning into worried. I can see a version where I'm fine, but I can see the other one too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Pinwheel do you think is most at risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lewis, our junior, is quicker with the tools and cheaper. Farah's senior and owns the place. I'm the one in the middle who's good but not special, and that's the seat that goes when an agency trims.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start looking for another job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not straight away. I'd want to be the one who can do the AI menu work and also deal with chefs face to face, because owners still want someone to argue with about colours. If after a year it's clear Pinwheel's shrinking, then I'd look at bigger studios in the city.

say: We need to **master the tools** before our restaurant clients do.
Jobs will **change rather than vanish**, like they did when phones got good cameras.
think: Menu writing, price updates and print orders are the **thinking tasks** AI takes first.
I'm the **middle designer** at Pinwheel, the seat that goes when an agency trims.
do: Take Farah's **two-evening course** on the newer design tools.
Learn **vinyl and sign fitting** from Marco the printer as hands-on backup.
Skip the summer trip and **save that money** instead.
feel: Uneasy turning into **worried**; she can picture both a fine version and a bad one.
S1.quote: If a café owner can type their dishes into an app and get a decent menu, my boss Farah won't need three designers, and I'm the middle one.
fieldNote: She mapped the card's task list straight onto her own week: **menu text, price changes**, print orders.
Her public line about cameras is calmer than her private sense of being the **expendable middle**.
The vinyl-fitting idea shows she's looking for the **hands-on edge** of her job.

steps.text: Enrol in the two-evening design tools course this spring
Shadow Marco on vinyl sign fitting on Saturdays
Put the summer trip money into the savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say something like, well, at least we all go down together. At work there'd be a lot of nervous jokes. Online I'd share whatever the design unions were saying, because I wouldn't know what else to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think my job is gone within a year or so of that. Logos, layouts and menus are all screen work, and a design can be done perfectly by something that doesn't need a salary. The only bit left would be fitting the signs and talking to owners, and that's not a full wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd stop spending on anything that isn't rent and food, and push my savings from four months to six if I can. I'd go full in on the sign fitting and install side with Marco, because robots for that are three years behind, so that's three years of work. And Tom and I would have the hard talk about moving somewhere cheaper, maybe nearer his parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. Two years is no time at all when you've just got your career going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens with your partner's job in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom's work is hands-on, he's literally fixing people's knees, so the card says he's got until about 2031. So our plan would be his wage carries the rent while I find my footing. I don't love that, but it's better than both of us panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually say to Farah and Marco?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Marco straight whether he'd take me on part time as a fitter. I'd tell Farah I'm grateful and I'd stay as long as she can pay me. And I'd look at signwriting by hand, because maybe people would pay extra for a human brushstroke for a while.

say: At least we'd **all go down together**, with plenty of nervous jokes at work.
I'd share what the **design unions** were saying, since I'd have nothing better.
think: My **job is gone** within about a year, because menus and logos are all screen work.
Sign fitting and owner meetings would be **left over**, but that isn't a full wage.
do: Cut spending to **rent and food** and stretch savings from four months to six.
Ask Marco for **part-time fitting work**, using the three years before robots arrive.
Talk with Tom about **moving somewhere cheaper**, maybe nearer his parents.
feel: **Scared**, because two years feels like no time at the start of a career.
S2.quote: Logos, layouts and menus are all screen work, and a design can be done perfectly by something that doesn't need a salary.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose the job** outright and leans on her partner's hands-on work as the bridge.
The three-year robot gap became her plan: **fitting and installing** signs.
She dislikes **depending on Tom** but accepts it as better than panic.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent, food and bills only
Build savings from four months to six
Ask Marco for part-time work fitting signs
Look at renting near Tom's parents to lower costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's use them, rather than doom about it. I'd probably say it to Lewis too, because he'd be spiralling. Online I'd keep it to sharing courses and job posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I said with the fast one, the design screen work ends, just in 2031 instead. The difference is I'd have time to build the second string properly instead of grabbing whatever Marco can give me. Five years is long enough to learn a trade and short enough that I can't waste one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd start a part-time sign-making and installation course at the college, the one-year certificate. I'd keep working at Pinwheel and use AI more on the menu work so I'm useful until the end. By year three I'd want to be doing install jobs on weekends, and by 2031 I'd move over fully, with savings at six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried but with a plan, which is a lot better than the fast one. I still don't like where it ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it change your plans with Tom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom would want to buy a flat in about three years. I'd say no, not until my work's on solid ground, because a mortgage on one secure wage feels reckless. We'd probably argue about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't sign fitting also going to robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but it's my lane for a while, not forever. Robots for hands-on work come around 2034 in this version, so it buys me three more years. I'd have to keep looking ahead even then.

say: We've got **a few years**, so let's use them instead of dooming about it.
I'd mostly share **courses and job posts** online, and calm Lewis down at work.
think: The **design screen work** still ends, just in 2031 instead of 2028.
Five years is long enough to **learn a trade** but too short to waste one.
do: Start the one-year **sign-making certificate** at the college this year.
Use AI more on **menu work** to stay useful at Pinwheel until the end.
Do **weekend install jobs** by year three and move over fully by 2031.
feel: **Worried** but with a **plan**, which feels far better than the two-year version.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to learn a trade and short enough that I can't waste one of them.
fieldNote: The extra time turns panic into a **staged plan**: course now, weekend installs, full switch later.
She'd put off **buying a flat** with Tom until her own income is steady.
She knows the hands-on lane is a **three-year reprieve**, not a safe harbour.

steps.text: Start the one-year sign-making certificate at the college
Use AI on menu updates to stay useful at Pinwheel
Put off buying a flat with Tom until work is steady
Get savings up to six months before switching jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a whole career change, so nobody needs to panic yet. At work I'd say it as a joke about retiring at 37. Online I wouldn't say much at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still think it's the end of design as a job for someone like me, just later. But by 2036 I'd be 37, and that's a normal age to have changed careers anyway. My partner Tom's mum retrained as a nurse at 40.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't jump. I'd stay at Pinwheel and use the AI tools as they come in, maybe take a project-lead role if Farah offers it. Around year three or four I'd do the sign-making course and start doing installs on the side. I'd keep saving, and we'd probably still buy the flat, just a smaller one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than scared. It's far enough off that I can think straight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think you'll be doing in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People still want things fitted, painted and put up, and someone has to stand in a café and say the sign goes there, not there. Maybe that's me, maybe it's something I haven't thought of yet. I'd keep my eyes open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does a decade change anything about family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably try for a baby around 32, which was the plan anyway. I'd just want my second career sorted before 2036, not halfway through it.

say: Ten years is **a whole career change**, so nobody needs to panic yet.
I'd joke at work about **retiring at 37** and say little online.
think: Design for someone like me still **ends**, just later on.
Changing careers by **37** is normal, like Tom's mum retraining as a nurse at forty.
do: Stay at Pinwheel and take a **project-lead role** if Farah offers one.
Do the **sign-making course** around year three or four, with installs on the side.
Keep saving and still **buy a smaller flat** with Tom.
feel: **Uneasy** rather than scared, because the date is far enough off to think straight.
S4.quote: By 2036 I'd be 37, and that's a normal age to have changed careers anyway. My partner Tom's mum retrained as a nurse at 40.
fieldNote: She still expects her design job to **go**, so the outcome is the same; only the pace eases.
A decade lets her keep **family plans**, including a baby around 32.
She pulls from family examples to make **career change** feel ordinary.

steps.text: Stay at Pinwheel and pick up the AI tools as they land
Ask Farah about a project-lead role on restaurant accounts
Take the sign-making course around year four
Buy a smaller flat with Tom and plan a baby around 32

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily, because there's no time to build anything and I'd be leaning on Tom while I scrambled. What would help is a paid way to retrain, like a part-time course where you get some wage while you learn, and some proper notice from employers instead of finding out on a Friday.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much of this is about the clients and not us. If restaurants are struggling, nobody's hiring designers anyway. Look after the small businesses and the design jobs mostly look after themselves.

headlineQuote: If restaurants are struggling, nobody's hiring designers anyway. Look after the small businesses and the design jobs mostly look after themselves.
portrait: Aisha is a 27-year-old designer at **Pinwheel Studio**, doing menus, signs and logos for cafés and restaurants.
She rents with **Tom**, a physio, and has about **four months** of savings she guards closely.
Her everyday worry is **restaurants closing**, which threatens her work even if AI stalls.
As AGI gets closer, she plans a move into **sign fitting**, using the three-year robot gap.
Pragmatic and steady, she uses AI **now and then** and moves once others have proven the path.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to build a second career and she'd lean on Tom.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining**, like a part-time course with some wage while she learns.
Proper **notice from employers** instead of finding out on a Friday.
